summary: Lists the link numbers assigned for use with the ARPANET host-host protocol, modifying the official protocol and replacing RFC 377. It was itself replaced by RFC 739.

eli5.summary: Computers need agreed numbers for different kinds of conversations. This is the list of which number means what. A later list replaced it.

questions: what links are reserved in arpanet
subtitle: Assigning link numbers for ARPANET protocol connections

tldr.problem: The ARPANET host-to-host protocol needs a standardized way to distinguish different types of communication channels between computers.
tldr.mechanism: Link numbers (0-255) are assigned by category: control (0), data connections (2-71), experiments in internetworking (155-158) and message switching (192-195), network measurements (159-191), and private experimental use (196-255).
tldr.outcome: This provided the formal registry for ARPANET link assignments. The numbering scheme was later updated and superseded by RFC 739.

today: RFC 604 has Unknown status. It was replaced by RFC 739, which updated the link number assignments further.

sections.title: Link Numbers for the ARPANET
sections.content:
The ARPANET host-to-host protocol allows communication between computers using link numbers to distinguish different types and purposes of connections. Link 0 is reserved for control traffic. Links 2 through 71 are available for ordinary data connections between hosts. Other ranges are reserved for specific experiments, measurements, and future use.

This RFC officially assigns link number ranges and updates the earlier assignment in RFC 317.
sections.eli5: Computers pick a link number to identify what they are talking about. Some numbers are for data, some for tests, and some for future experiments.

sections.title: Link Number Assignments
sections.content: Link 0 is the control link for protocol management. Links 1 and 72-154 are reserved for future development. Links 2-71 are available for normal connections. Links 155-158 are designated for experiments with the Internetworking Protocol developed by Kahn and Cerf. Links 159-191 are assigned for measurements conducted by the Network Measurement Center at UCLA. Links 192-195 are allocated for Message Switching Protocol experiments. Links 196-255 are open for private experimental use.
sections.eli5: The range is divided up: some for normal traffic, some for testing new ideas, some for measuring the network, and some left over for anyone to use in their own experiments.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content: Early ARPANET software needed to multiplex multiple logical conversations over a single host-to-host connection. The link number field in the protocol identified each logical conversation's purpose. By assigning ranges for control traffic, data, and experiments, this RFC provided structure that allowed hosts to distinguish and route different types of traffic correctly. The experiments in internetworking and message switching were especially important for testing new protocols that would eventually lead to the Internet.
sections.eli5: Link numbers let one connection between two computers carry many different kinds of traffic at once, each marked so the computers know what each message is for.

references.text: Postel, J., "Assigned Link Numbers", RFC 317, NIC 9347, March 1972.
